title: What Is Original Sin? Three Christian Traditions
subtitle: Original sin and how far the damage reaches. Three faithful traditions, each given its own strongest voice.
triageNote: That humanity is fallen and needs rescue is near the heart of the faith. The exact mechanics of how Adam's sin reaches us divide faithful traditions, and a believer can love God with all their mind and still land in a different place than the believer in the next pew.
question:
When the first man turned away from God in the garden, what exactly did the rest of us inherit. A wounded nature that pulls us toward wrong. The legal guilt of his act, charged to our account before we draw a breath. Only death and a broken world we are born into. The Bible says we are all caught in something that started before us, but it does not spell out the wiring in a single tidy sentence. So the church has read the same passages and reached three honest answers.

The question is older than the labels we now hang on it. It came to a head in the early fifth century, when a British monk named Pelagius taught in Rome that human beings are born morally neutral, able to keep God's commands by the unaided strength of the will, and that Adam's sin harmed no one but Adam by way of a bad example. Augustine of Hippo answered that the harm runs in the blood of the race, that we are born already turned away and unable to turn back without grace. The church sided with Augustine against Pelagius at the Council of Carthage in 418 and again, more carefully, at the Second Council of Orange in 529, which condemned the idea that we can take the first step toward God on our own. Those councils settled that we are fallen and cannot save ourselves. They did not settle the exact mechanism by which Adam's fall reaches each of us, and that is the unsettled ground the three views below still work.

Notice what the dispute is and is not. No faithful tradition says we arrive clean and merely pick up bad habits later. That is the Pelagian road the whole church closed. The live question is narrower and more precise. Do we inherit Adam's corruption only, the disordered nature, or do we also inherit his guilt, the legal verdict for his act, reckoned to us before we have done anything at all. And underneath even that lies a question about death itself, whether what came down to us is first of all a courtroom sentence or first of all a wound, a mortality that then breeds the sins each of us commits. Three traditions, reading the same Genesis and the same Romans, weigh those words differently.
whyItMatters:
This is not a puzzle for specialists. How deep the problem goes decides how big a rescue we need.

If the damage is only a bad environment and some poor examples, then what we need is better teaching, firmer rules, a community that shows us a better way. We need a coach. But if the damage reaches into the will itself, into the part of us that chooses, then no amount of coaching reaches the place that is broken. We need something done to us from outside, not just shown to us. We need a rescuer. This is exactly the fork the church faced when Pelagius said the will is healthy and only needs the right example, and Augustine answered that the will itself is the patient on the table. The whole doctrine of grace turns on which is true.

The fall is the name the church gives to that first turning away, the moment in Genesis 3 when the first human beings chose their own way over God's. The whole human story bent. Original sin is the name the Western church settled on for whatever came down to us from that moment, the condition we are born into rather than the wrongs we later commit. The Eastern church preferred a different name, ancestral sin, and the difference in the name carries a difference in the doctrine, as you will see below. The three views all agree that something came down from Adam. They disagree about what came down, whether a wound only or a wound and a verdict, and they disagree about how it travels, whether by Adam standing as our legal representative or by our springing from him as a corrupted source.

The size of the answer is the size of the gospel. Watch how it works. If Adam's one act is charged to all who descend from him, then the way God deals with the whole race through a single representative is already established before Christ ever comes, and the cross can then charge Christ's one act of obedience to all who are joined to him. Take the first half away and you may weaken the second. That is why the Reformers held the doctrine so tightly. They saw imputation as the rail the gospel itself runs on.

Get this wrong in one direction and you make God a tyrant who condemns newborns for a crime committed before they existed, a charge the church has wrestled with at least since the question of unbaptized infants pressed on Augustine himself. Get it wrong in the other direction and you make sin a surface stain, easily washed, the will basically intact, the cross an overreaction to a problem we could have managed with effort. Both errors shrink something that must not be shrunk. One shrinks the justice and goodness of God. The other shrinks the depth of our need and the cost of the remedy. The three faithful views below are each, in their own way, trying to keep both from shrinking at once.

positions.name: The Augustinian and Reformed View
positions.inOneLine: We fell in Adam, inheriting both a corrupted nature and the guilt of his sin charged to our account.
positions.bestCase:
Let me tell you what I see when I read my own heart honestly. I do not have to teach a child to lie. I have to teach a child to tell the truth. The bent is there from the start, before any bad influence, before any choice. Scripture names this and I will not flinch from it. When David says he was sinful from the time his mother conceived him, in Psalm 51:5, he is not blaming his mother. He is confessing that the rot goes all the way down and all the way back. Paul names it too. He says we were by nature children of wrath, in Ephesians 2, by nature, not by mere habit picked up along the way.

I stand in a long line. Augustine of Hippo argued exactly this against Pelagius, who taught that we are born clean and need only good examples to do right. The church agreed with Augustine, not with Pelagius, at the Council of Carthage in 418 and again at the Second Council of Orange in 529, which denied that we can take even the first step toward God without grace going before us. Calvin gathered up Augustine's insight, Jonathan Edwards defended it with great care in his treatise on original sin, and the Westminster Confession, the Belgic Confession, and the Canons of Dort confess it as the settled teaching of the Reformed churches. I am not inventing a harsh doctrine. I am receiving one the church tested over centuries.

I hold to total depravity. Let me define that carefully, because the name is often misheard. Total depravity does not mean we are as bad as we could possibly be, or that every person is a monster, or that unbelievers can do nothing kind. It means sin has touched every part of us, the mind, the will, the affections, the body. There is no clean corner of the self from which we could lift ourselves out. The disease is not in one organ. It is in the bloodstream. Romans 3 sweeps over throat and tongue and lips and feet and eyes, every faculty pressed into the service of sin, and concludes that no one seeks God. Sin reaches the will too. That is why I say we cannot, on our own, turn and choose God. The drowning man does not need swimming lessons. He needs to be pulled out.

Now the harder part, and I hold it because I believe Scripture teaches it. I believe Adam's guilt itself is charged to us. Here I need two terms. Imputation means to credit something to a person's account, to reckon it as theirs in the eyes of the law. Think of a debt transferred onto a balance sheet. Federal headship means Adam stood as the representative of the whole human race, the way the head of a household or the head of a nation acts on behalf of all under him. What he did, he did for us. When Adam fell, we fell, because he was acting as us. (Some in my tradition, following Augustine and Jonathan Edwards, have explained the link a second way, by what is called seminal headship, the idea that the whole race was somehow really present in Adam as in a seed, so that his act was truly ours. Federal headship is the cleaner account, but both are trying to honor the same text.) This sounds harsh until you see the glory hidden in it. The whole logic of salvation runs on the same rail. Just as Adam's one act was charged to all who are in him, so Christ's one act of obedience is charged to all who are in him. Romans 5 sets the two heads side by side on purpose, and verses 18 and 19 make the parallel exact. As by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. If you take away my imputation of Adam's sin, I fear you have also pulled the floor out from under the imputation of Christ's righteousness. Then where is my hope on the last day. I do not want to be saved by my own improvement. I want to be saved by a righteousness reckoned to me that I did not earn. The same machinery that condemns me in Adam is the machinery that rescues me in Christ.

What of Ezekiel 18, which says the son will not bear the guilt of the father. I do not run from it. Ezekiel is answering a proverb the exiles used to dodge responsibility for their own sins, the sour grapes the fathers ate that supposedly set the children's teeth on edge. God tells them each generation answers for its own covenant unfaithfulness and cannot hide behind the last. That is a true word about fathers and sons within Israel. It is a different category from Adam, who is not merely my distant father but the appointed head of the entire race, the one man through whom death came to all. Headship over all humanity is not the same relation as parent to child, and Paul, who surely knew Ezekiel, still wrote Romans 5.

So I say it plainly. We are guilty before we are guilty of anything we did. And the answer is not that we are better than that. The answer is a second Adam.

positions.name: The Wesleyan and Arminian View
positions.inOneLine: We inherit a corrupted nature and cannot save ourselves. But grace that comes before any choice is given to all, so no one is finally lost for Adam's sin alone.
positions.bestCase:
I begin where my Reformed brother begins. And I want you to hear that I do not soften the diagnosis. We inherit a fallen, corrupted nature from Adam. I believe in what the old writers called concupiscence, the disordered desire we are born with. It is the inward pull toward the wrong thing, there before we ever act on it. Left to myself, I am truly unable to turn to God. On my own strength I am dead in my sins, exactly as Ephesians 2 says. A dead man does not raise himself. So far my brother and I are walking the same road, and I want that understood, because Arminians are too often slandered as half Pelagians. We are not. Jacob Arminius affirmed original sin and the bondage of the fallen will, and John Wesley wrote a long treatise on original sin against the optimism of his own century, insisting that humanity by nature is dead in sin and wholly corrupted. The Remonstrants who carried Arminius forward confessed the same. We affirm Carthage and Orange. We deny that we can take the first step toward God on our own. Pelagius is no friend of ours.

We part company with the Reformed over what God does about the fall, and for whom. I hold to prevenient grace. Prevenient simply means coming before. It is the grace God gives ahead of any decision on our part, grace that goes before us and wakes the dead will enough that a real response becomes possible. I do not believe any human being is left in pure nature, abandoned to the fall with no help. The true light that enlightens everyone coming into the world, the Father who draws, the Spirit who convicts the world of sin, these reach every person. So the ability to respond to God is never something we generate from inside ourselves. It is always a gift, always grace first. On that point I stand shoulder to shoulder with my Reformed brother against any teaching that we save ourselves. The difference is that I believe this awakening grace is given to all, not secretly to some, and that it can be finally resisted.

Here is the hinge. Because grace comes to all, I do not believe anyone is finally condemned for Adam's sin by itself. The inherited corruption is real and it would be enough to ruin us, but God has not left it to run its course unopposed. So when a person is at last lost, it is for their own sin, their own refusal of the grace that came to find them. It is not for a verdict handed down at birth for a deed they had no part in. I cannot square a final condemnation for Adam's guilt alone with the God who so loved the world that he gave his Son, the God who is not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance. Ezekiel 18:20 rings in my ears, that the soul who sins is the one who will die and the son will not bear the guilt of the father. Guilt, to me, attaches to the one who refuses grace, not to the newborn. And I will say honestly where this presses on me. The Reformed reading of Romans 5:18 and 19 is strong, the many made sinners by one man's act. My answer is that the Adam side names the universal ruin and the Christ side names the grace held out just as universally, the trespass abounding and grace abounding all the more, so that the verdict of condemnation is real but is met, for every person, by an offer of life.

This is also where free will enters. Let me define it as I mean it. I do not mean a will that is neutral or self powered, the Pelagian will that needs no grace. I mean a will that grace has freed enough to say yes or no to God. The rescuer sets it free, so the response is genuinely ours and genuinely a gift at the same time. Wesley called this the cooperation of grace, not a partnership of equals but a wounded patient given strength enough to reach for the physician. So I preach to every person without exception, and I preach with confidence, because I believe there is grace already at work in every person I am preaching to. No one is outside the reach of the offer. No one I address is beyond hope.

positions.name: The Eastern Orthodox Ancestral Sin View
positions.inOneLine: From Adam we inherit death, mortality, and a wounded nature, but not his personal guilt. Guilt is not the kind of thing that can be passed down.
positions.bestCase:
I want to start by changing one word. The word carries a whole theology with it. In the West you speak of original sin. We in the East speak of ancestral sin. Ancestral sin means the sin of our ancestor Adam and what it set loose in the world, chiefly death and corruption, the unraveling of a nature made for life. The shift in the word is the shift in the whole picture. What Adam handed down to us is not a verdict. It is a wound, and a corpse waiting to happen. I would add gently that this is not a late Eastern novelty. It is how the Greek Fathers read the Scriptures from the beginning, before Augustine, in a tradition that never passed through the Latin translation that shaped the Western debate.

Here is what I believe we inherit. I do not make it small. We inherit mortality, the certainty of death. With death comes fear. Out of the fear of death comes the whole tangle of grasping, self protecting sin, the man clutching at security because he knows he is dying. We inherit a nature knocked off its axis, weakened, inclined to passions it cannot govern. The image of God in us is darkened, though never erased, for that is the dignity no fall can take away. This is a real and grievous fall. We cannot heal it ourselves. So I too confess that we need a rescuer, and the rescue I look for is nothing less than Christ trampling down death by death, as we sing at Pascha. Athanasius taught that the Word became what we are so that we might be healed of corruption, and the Cappadocian Fathers carried that forward. The resurrection reaches back to undo the corruption Adam started. The remedy is not first a payment of a fine. It is the raising of the dead.

But I cannot follow the West in saying we inherit Adam's guilt. Guilt, as I understand it, is personal. It belongs to the one who did the deed and to the one who consents to it. It is not a substance, not a debt that can be wired from one account to another across the generations. Ezekiel says in chapter 18 that the soul who sins is the one who will die, and that the son will not bear the guilt of the father, and the father will not bear the guilt of the son. I take that as God himself telling us what kind of thing guilt is and what kind of thing it is not. A newborn has done nothing. To call that infant guilty seems to me to confuse the wound with the crime. The baby has inherited the disease. The baby has not inherited the verdict. This is also why the question of unbaptized infants, which so troubled Augustine in the Latin West, never pressed on us in the same way. We do not begin from a charge laid against the child.

This even reaches into how I read the famous line in Romans 5. The Western debate hangs on a small Greek phrase at the end of verse 12, eph ho. Augustine read it through an old Latin rendering as in whom, that is, in Adam all sinned, and he built the doctrine of inherited guilt on that reading. But the Greek Fathers spoke the language Paul wrote in, and they heard it as because, or with the result that. Death spread to all, and in that reign of death all of us went on to sin, each in our own person. Death is the inheritance. Sin is what each of us then does inside the kingdom of death. When Paul says in verse 19 that the many were made sinners, I read made not as a verdict charged to us but as constituted, the whole race set on a death bound course in which each person then sins. So I hold the fall with full seriousness and still say, with a clear conscience, that I was born mortal and wounded but not yet condemned. Christ came not first to pay a charge against my account but to raise a dying race back to life.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: This is the battleground text, claimed by all three, and the hinge is the translation of one phrase in verse 12.
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul draws a long comparison between two men who each act on behalf of many. Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world and death through sin, and death spread to everyone. Through one man, Christ, came an act of righteousness that brings life to many. The two heads stand opposite each other. The whole flow of condemnation and grace runs through them.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: The hard question for everyone is the end of verse 12, the Greek phrase eph ho. The Augustinian reading takes it to mean in whom, that is, in Adam all sinned. That supports inherited guilt. The Eastern and much modern reading takes it to mean because, or with the result that, that is, death spread to all and so all sinned personally. That removes inherited guilt from the verse. An older Latin translation rendered it in whom, and Augustine built heavily on that Latin, which later readers argued was a translation pressed too far.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reader says the surrounding logic settles it. Paul keeps insisting that the many were made sinners and condemned through the one man's single act, before they had done anything. One sin brought condemnation to all. That only makes sense if Adam's act is reckoned to us. The Wesleyan reader agrees Adam's act ruined the race but reads the same verses through prevenient grace. The condemnation in Adam is answered by grace given to all in Christ, abounding even more than the trespass. The Orthodox reader says the chapter is about the reign of death and life, not a ledger of imputed guilt. The Greek Fathers who spoke the language natively heard because, not in whom.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Augustinian and Reformed, as the clearest statement that the corruption reaches back to conception.
biblicalEvidence.summary: David, confessing his sin with Bathsheba, says he was brought forth in iniquity and that in sin his mother conceived him. He traces his guilt not merely to his recent act but to his very beginning.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for any view that wants to treat sin as only learned behavior or only adult choices. David reaches back before birth. Some critics also read it as Hebrew poetry, strong overstatement for the weight of confession rather than a doctrinal claim about conception.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reader takes it nearly at face value as inherited sinfulness from the first moment. The Wesleyan reader agrees it shows a corrupt nature present from conception, which is exactly the inherited corruption they affirm. They deny it proves inherited guilt. The Orthodox reader hears the inherited mortality and the wounded nature in the verse. He reads it as poetic confession of a condition, not a statement that the infant bears Adam's personal guilt.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The depth of the problem, shared ground for all three on our inability to save ourselves.
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul tells the believers they were dead in trespasses and sins, walking in them, and were by nature children of wrath like everyone else. The word dead is the weight of it. Not sick, not weak, but dead.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hardest for any view that makes the human will basically healthy and able to choose God unaided. Dead people do not revive themselves. The phrase by nature children of wrath is hard for the Orthodox view, since it sounds like a wrath resting on us from birth.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reader takes dead in the fullest sense, the will included, so that only God's prior work can raise us. That fits total depravity. The Wesleyan reader fully agrees we are dead and unable, then adds that prevenient grace is precisely God's raising work offered to all. The deadness is real but not the last word. The Orthodox reader reads dead as the reign of death and corruption over us. He reads children of wrath as our actual condition and conduct under death, not a guilt charged from Adam. Paul says by nature and then immediately points to how they walked.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The shared foundation, the account of the fall itself that all three are trying to interpret.
biblicalEvidence.summary: The first humans, tempted, eat the forbidden fruit. Shame, hiding, blame, and a curse follow. They are put out of the garden and barred from the tree of life. Death enters the world. This is the event every view calls the fall.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: The chapter itself never uses the later vocabulary of imputation, federal headship, or inherited guilt. That is hard for any view that wants its precise doctrine to be simply stated here. It also raises the question of the historical Adam, which presses on every view that builds the inheritance on a real first man.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reader sees Adam as the covenant head whose fall is the fall of all. The curse and the barred tree of life signal the death now passed to his children. The Wesleyan reader sees the same ruin entering. But he reads the promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent as grace already breaking in for all. The Orthodox reader fixes on the loss of the tree of life and the entry of death and corruption as the core inheritance, the wound rather than the verdict. He reads the chapter as the beginning of the long story of death undone in Christ.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The universality of sin, shared ground, and a particular support for total depravity.
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul stacks up a chain of quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah. No one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God, all have turned away. He describes throats, tongues, lips, mouths, feet, eyes, every part pressed into the service of sin.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for any view that holds some people naturally seek God on their own. Paul says no one does. It can seem hard for the Wesleyan view, which insists people can respond to God, until prevenient grace is brought in.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reader notes how the passage sweeps over every body part and faculty and hears total depravity, sin touching the whole person. The Wesleyan reader fully agrees that no one seeks God in their natural state, which is just why prevenient grace must come first to enable any seeking. The passage describes nature apart from grace, not nature as grace has touched it. The Orthodox reader reads it as the description of humanity under the dominion of death and the passions, universal corruption that needs healing, again without requiring inherited personal guilt.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The Orthodox and Wesleyan views, as the clearest statement that guilt is personal and not inherited.
biblicalEvidence.summary: The prophet declares that the soul who sins is the one who will die. The son will not bear the guilt of the father, and the father will not bear the guilt of the son. The righteousness of the righteous will be on himself, and the wickedness of the wicked on himself.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: This is the sharpest thorn for the Augustinian view of inherited guilt, since on its face it denies that one person bears another's guilt. The Reformed reader must explain how imputation of Adam's sin survives this verse.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Orthodox reader takes it straight as proof that guilt is personal and cannot be transferred, which is the heart of the ancestral sin position. The Wesleyan reader likewise hears confirmation that final guilt attaches to a person's own response, not to Adam's deed. The Reformed reader answers that Ezekiel is addressing a specific proverb the exiles used to dodge responsibility for their own sins under God's covenant dealings with Israel. Its point is that each generation cannot blame the last for its own punishment. It is not aimed at the unique representative role of Adam over the whole race, which is a different category of headship than father to son.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Augustinian and Reformed, the tightest link between Adam's one act and the condemnation of all.
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul says that as one trespass led to condemnation for all, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all. As by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: The parallel is hard for the Orthodox view. Made sinners through Adam's disobedience sounds like more than inherited mortality. It presses the Wesleyan view to explain how condemnation for all is answered without inherited guilt.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Reformed reader sees the cleanest case for imputation, the many made sinners by one man's act exactly as the many are made righteous by another's. The two imputations are matched. The Wesleyan reader holds the Adam side as the universal ruin that grace universally answers, reading the all who are justified as the offer extended to all. The Orthodox reader reads made sinners as constituted as a sinful, death bound race that then sins in person, and made righteous as constituted alive in Christ. The parallel stays about the two states of the race, not about a transferred verdict.

weighing:
What follows is my own judgment, offered tentatively and held loosely, and I would be glad to be corrected by any of the three teachers above. I am weighing, not refereeing, and the three are wiser than I am.

I find myself most persuaded that the inheritance is real and deep. It reaches the will, not merely our circumstances. Ephesians 2 says we were dead, not weak, and Romans 3 says no one seeks God, and those are hard to read any softer than that. Let me underline the point. All three views actually agree on this. The Reformed, the Wesleyan, and the Orthodox all confess that we cannot save ourselves and that grace must come first. The whole church said as much against Pelagius at Carthage in 418 and at Orange in 529. I think that shared ground matters more than the family argument that follows it. Whatever else is true, I cannot lift myself out, and I need grace before I can even want grace. That is the load bearing truth, and it is not actually in dispute among these three. Losing it, sliding back toward Pelagius and a self that can fix itself, would be the real danger.

On the disputed question of inherited guilt, I confess I feel the pull of both sides and I have not made peace between them. The Reformed reading of Romans 5:18 and 19 is strong. The link it preserves between Adam's one act and Christ's one act is not a small thing to give up, because the same logic that hands me Adam's ruin hands me Christ's righteousness, and I do not want to weaken the rail my salvation rides on. Yet Ezekiel 18:20 weighs on me, and the Greek reading of eph ho in Romans 5:12 as because rather than in whom is at least as defensible as the Latin reading Augustine leaned on, perhaps more so, given that the Greek Fathers spoke Paul's own language. The Reformed answer, that Ezekiel addresses fathers and sons in Israel while Adam is the unique head of the whole race, is a fair distinction and I take it seriously. The Orthodox answer, that guilt is simply not the kind of thing that transfers, is also weighty. If I had to say where I lean today, it would be toward holding the corruption with both hands and holding the imputed guilt with an open one. I am willing to let Scripture pry my fingers either way. The Wesleyan instinct, that no one is finally lost except by refusing grace they were actually given, is the pastoral note I keep returning to, and I grant in fairness that it must answer the Romans 5 parallel with care rather than waving it off.

What I am sure of is the shape of the answer, even where I am unsure of the mechanism. However the damage reaches us, whether as a transferred verdict or only as a wound and a death, it reaches us before we choose. And so the rescue must come to us before we choose. A coach will not do. A better example will not do. We needed a second Adam, one who could stand for the race as the first one did and undo what he did, and that is exactly what we have. On the size of the rescue the three teachers do not disagree at all.
charitableDisagreement:
If you are a new believer reading this, hear me carefully. A faithful Christian can hold any of these three and love the same Lord, read the same Bible, kneel at the same cross. Augustine, Wesley, and the Greek Fathers are not enemies across a battlefield. They are family arguing at the same table about a grief they all feel, the wreckage Adam left and how far the cracks run. Each of them is trying to honor a real strand of Scripture. The Augustinian is guarding the parallel between the two Adams and refusing to let our salvation rest on our own improvement. The Wesleyan is guarding the goodness of God toward every person and the truth that grace reaches all. The Orthodox is guarding the personal nature of guilt and the picture of Christ as the one who raises the dead, not only the one who pays a fine. Notice that each is protecting something the others would not want to lose either. When you find yourself drawn to one, resist the urge to make the other two villains. Steelman the view you reject until you can state it so well its holders would nod and say yes, that is what we believe.

It helps to remember the real heretic in this story. It was Pelagius, who said we are born clean and can save ourselves by trying harder, and the whole church, East and West, condemned him together at Carthage and at Orange. All three of these traditions stand on the same side of that line. Their argument with one another is a household argument among people who already agree that we are fallen and helpless and in need of grace before we can lift a finger. That is a very different thing from the argument the church actually had with Pelagius.

Is this a hill to die on. No, and yes, depending on the hill. We are fallen. The problem reaches into us and not just around us, and we cannot save ourselves and need a rescuer from outside. That much is near the heart of the faith and worth defending to the last breath. The exact mechanism, whether Adam's guilt is imputed to us or only his corruption and death are inherited, and whether eph ho in Romans 5:12 means in whom or because, is a second order question. The church has lived with honest disagreement there for many centuries without breaking fellowship over it, and entire communions, Reformed and Methodist and Orthodox, have held their different answers while confessing the same creeds. Hold the first thing with conviction. Hold the second with charity. Do not break communion with a brother over the wiring of a doctrine you both confess leaves you needing the very same grace, dependent on the very same cross.

relatedDebates.topic: Soteriology and the bondage or freedom of the will
relatedDebates.note: How deep the fall reaches drives the whole doctrine of salvation. If the will itself is in bondage, then God must act first and decisively. That leads toward the Reformed account of grace. If grace frees the will to a real yes or no, you get the Wesleyan account. Augustine argued it with Pelagius, and Luther with Erasmus over the bondage of the will, the same argument seen from the salvation side.

relatedDebates.topic: Whether infants who die are saved
relatedDebates.note: This is where the views feel their weight pastorally. If Adam's guilt is imputed, the tradition has had to work hard to give assurance about infants who die, often appealing to God's mercy and covenant promise. The Wesleyan stress on grace given to all and the Orthodox denial of inherited guilt both ease the question in their own way. Most in every tradition today affirm hope for such children. But the reasoning differs by view.

All three views as classically stated assume a real first human being whose act sets the human story off course. Recent discussion about human origins presses the question. Does the doctrine of the fall require a single historical Adam, or can it be carried by other readings of Genesis. How a believer answers this shapes how the inheritance is even said to travel from him to us.
